title: Katakana
subtitle: The 46 basic characters of the angular syllabary

cards.note: An axe with the blade on top and the handle falling down to the left: a for axe. In マ (ma) the second stroke is only a short tick.
It's the left half of the kanji 伊, which it comes from: a person leaning on a post. Sounds like the ee in "eagle".
Like hiragana う but angular: a roof with a chimney, under which someone groans "ooh". Without the chimney it looks close to ラ (ra).
A steel girder seen from the side, like an elevator shaft: e for elevator. It looks just like the kanji 工 (craft).
An old man leaning forward on his cane, saying "oh!". Compare ホ (ho), which has two little legs instead of one slanted stroke.
Almost like hiragana か, just without the little stroke on the right. It also looks like the kanji 力 (power).
A key with two teeth: ki. It's hiragana き without the curve at the bottom.
A cuckoo's beak opening to the left, calling "ku ku". In ワ (wa) the roof is flat and there's a wall on the left.
Looks like a tilted letter K: ke. The third stroke hangs down freely, while in ク (ku) the strokes are joined.
A corner like a box open to the left: ko. In ユ (yu) the bottom stroke is longer and sticks out.
A crossbar on two posts, the right one bending down to the left: sa. Picture a saddle on two legs.
The two short strokes are stacked on the left and the long one sweeps up from the bottom. In ツ (tsu) the short strokes sit side by side on top and the long one falls downward.
Like a coat hanger with one leg kicked out: su. In ヌ (nu) an extra stroke crosses the curve.
Like hiragana せ, just with an angular hook instead of a curve: se.
Short stroke at the top left, the long one falls from the top right: so. In ン (n) the long stroke rises from the bottom upward.
Like ク (ku) with a small stroke in the middle: ta.
Like キ (ki) but the top stroke is slanted like a hat: chi. テ (te), by contrast, has two straight horizontal lines.
Two short strokes side by side on top, the long one falls from the top right: tsu. In シ (shi) the short strokes are stacked on the left.
A TV antenna on a roof, and TV in Japanese is テレビ (terebi): te.
A post with a small branch to the right, like a totem pole: to. It has just two strokes.
A cross whose vertical stroke curves down to the left, like a knife, which is ナイフ (naifu) in Japanese: na.
Two horizontal lines, just like the number two, 二, which is read ni.
Like ス (su) with an extra stroke crossing it, like chopsticks in a bowl of noodles: nu.
A person with outstretched arms under a roof, holding a net: ne.
A single slash, like a sweep that says no: no. It appears inside many other characters, for example メ (me).
Two strokes spreading apart like a laughing mouth: ha ha. It looks almost like the kanji 八 (eight).
A person leaning back and giggling "hee hee". The bottom stroke hooks off to the right.
A single hook like the slope of Mount Fuji: fu. Blow lightly through your lips, halfway between f and h.
Looks almost exactly like hiragana へ: a small hill. One of the few characters you get for free.
A cross with two little legs, like a wooden cross on a hill: ho. Compare オ (o), which has only one slanted stroke.
A big hook with a short tick below it, like a mask seen from the side: ma. In ア (a) the second stroke runs long and down.
Three slanted strokes stacked up, like three missiles flying: mi.
A triangle with a small nose on the right, like a cow's head going "moo": mu.
A slanted X, like a winking eye, and eye in Japanese is 目 (me).
Like hiragana も but angular, with two crossbars and a hook to the right: mo.
Like hiragana や without the small dot: ya. Picture a yak with one long horn.
Like a U lying on its side, with a longer bottom stroke that sticks out: yu. In コ (ko) the strokes end flush.
A backwards E, like a comb with three teeth pointing left: yo.
A short lid above a hook: ra. In ウ (u) there's a little chimney instead of the lid.
Almost exactly like hiragana り: two vertical strokes, the right one longer and curved.
Two legs, the right one kicking upward at the end: ru. リ (ri) has no kick.
A single stroke that bends up to the right at the bottom, like the right leg of ル (ru): re.
A square, almost like the kanji 口 (mouth): ro. The katakana is a little smaller.
A roof with a wall on the left and a curve going down: wa. ク (ku) has no wall.
Like フ (fu) with an extra horizontal stroke in the middle: wo. As a particle it's almost always written in hiragana, を.
A short stroke at the top left and a long one rising from the bottom: n. In ソ (so) the long stroke falls downward.
